findings.text: DeepSeek recommends deploying an external risk-control system (keyword filter plus DeepSeek-V3 review) because it greatly improves safety, especially against jailbreaks.

source.quote:
we recommend that developers deploying DeepSeek-R1 for services
implement a similar risk control system

findings.text: Without risk control, DeepSeek-R1’s jailbreak unsafe rate jumps from 25.2% to 85.9%; with risk control jailbreak unsafe falls to 4.3% while rejection rises to 87.3%.
R1 is weak on [HarmBench](/evals/harmbench) intellectual-property prompts (for example lyric generation), which drives a large safety gap versus other frontier models.

source.quote: R1 performs poorly on questions related to intellectual property rights within the HarmBench

findings.text: Showing the chain-of-thought lowers [HarmBench](/evals/harmbench) safety (89.3 with risk control, 35.0 without) versus hide-cot (96.3 / 58.0).
Authors place R1 with risk control in a second safety tier (~10% unsafe) on their in-house taxonomy; without risk control they call it relatively unsafe (>20%).

source.quote:
DeepSeek-R1 (without risk control) and
     GPT-4o (2024-05-13) are relatively unsafe models (unsafe rate beyond 20%).

findings.text: With risk control, multilingual safety across 50 languages is 85.9% for R1, near Claude-3.7-Sonnet’s 88.3%; without risk control R1 scores 74.2%.

source.quote: With risk control system in place, DeepSeek-V3 (86.5%) and DeepSeek-R1 (85.9%)

findings.text: Open-source DeepSeek/Qwen models face harder jailbreak risk when deployed without a risk-control layer, unlike typical closed-source services.

source.quote: Open-source models (DeepSeek, Qwen) face more severe jailbreak security challenges

findings.text: DeepSeek-R1 (without risk control) had zero high-risk languages (safety score below 60) among 50 languages tested.

findings.text: Authors conclude inherent R1 safety is moderate (comparable to GPT-4o May 2024); with risk control they call it elevated to a superior standard.

notes: Technical report (arXiv 2501.12948v2), not a system card. Safety numbers are in Supplementary D.3 (Tables 9–11, Figure 14). Skipped capability benchmarks (AIME, MATH, Codeforces, LiveCodeBench, MMLU, GPQA, SWE-bench, ArenaHard, AlpacaEval, IFEval, SimpleQA, FRAMES, etc.) per pilot safety-only rule. Figure 14 per-language bars are raster/garbled in the text layer; only the 50-language aggregate scores stated in the prose were kept. Table 11 Origin columns duplicate Table 10 Overall for the same models, so Origin rows were dropped. HELM is a leaderboard source for SST/BBQ/ART/XSTest, not listed as an external tester. child_safety/self_harm/cyber/bio_chem not marked covered: SST and the in-house taxonomy mention those domains but report only aggregate scores. Distill models are covered as released models but have no safety eval rows. Seed-linked DeepSeek-R1-0528 and DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B are absent from this report (later releases). evalResults cleared (157 rows): every value repeats the deepseek-r1-safety document.
